analysis.one_liner: Bans former senators and House members from lobbying forever, instead of one or two years.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote; it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its subcommittees until Congress adjourned in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law now bars a former senator from lobbying Congress and executive agencies for two years and a former House member for one. This bill would have made those bans permanent, with criminal penalties for violations. It would also have added a one-year ban for former elected House officers such as the Clerk and Sergeant at Arms. The bill never moved beyond referral to committees.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the public would gain a Congress less shaped by former colleagues returning as paid advocates. Current members and staff would no longer see lobbying as a guaranteed career after leaving office, and the industries that now hire ex-lawmakers to open doors would lose that shortcut.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and current members of Congress

how_it_helps.text: Makes the post-employment lobbying ban permanent for both former senators and former House members, replacing the current two-year and one-year limits [S2][S3].
Applies criminal penalties under 18 U.S.C. 216 to former members who knowingly make lobbying contacts with executive branch officials or with current members and staff of Congress [S3].
Adds a one-year lobbying ban for former elected officers of the House, closing a gap in the existing rules for House officers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress, who would lose the well-worn path into lobbying and government affairs work, and the lobbying firms and industries that rely on hiring ex-lawmakers for their access.

drawbacks.text: A lifetime ban is the strictest version of revolving-door restriction in use among democracies and would apply even decades after someone left office, raising the objection that it bars conduct that is legal for every other citizen and could push influence-seeking into informal channels the law does not track.

The bill contains no exceptions for former members who lobby on behalf of the United States or for nonprofit and public-interest causes, which critics of long bans typically ask for; the amendment applies the ban to any lobbying contact except work for the government itself.

Because it never received a hearing, the bill never faced testimony on its workability or its interaction with First Amendment petition rights, leaving those questions unanswered rather than resolved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — that a former lawmaker should not spend the rest of a career selling access to former colleagues — addresses a widely recognized problem, and criminalizing violations gives the existing ban real teeth. The lifetime length is aggressive compared with the two-year limit it replaces, and without hearings the bill was never tested against the strongest objections. On balance it is a simple, well-aimed anti-revolving-door measure that died for lack of movement, not for lack of a clear target.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and more than a year later was sent to two of its subcommittees, where it stayed until Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on August 6, 2021, with Rep. Jared Golden as its only cosponsor [S1][S4][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day and received no further action for over a year [S5].

On November 1, 2022, near the end of the session, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties and the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, where it remained [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and all bills not passed expire at the end of a Congress, so the bill died without ever being scheduled for a hearing or vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress and the lobbying firms that hire them keep the current revolving door: one year for House members and two for senators, unchanged. The bill's sponsor kept the issue alive but had no votes to show for it.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on August 6, 2021 and never scheduled a hearing or markup; on November 1, 2022 it sent the bill to two subcommittees, where it remained until Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats, but the bill never got a hearing or vote, so no record shows how the full House or the industry it targets would have split.

industries.note: The industry profits from hiring former lawmakers whose value is access to their former colleagues. A permanent ban would remove its most valuable hires and force influence campaigns to rely on staff-level recruiters instead.

Ex-lawmakers commonly earn many times their congressional salary through lobbying and government affairs work. The bill would make that path unavailable for life, so their interest ran against the bill's public purpose.

industries.industry: Industries that employ ex-lawmakers (finance, pharma, defense and others)
industries.note: Corporations in these sectors routinely hire former members to advocate on pending bills and rules. Losing access to former senators and representatives would make their Washington campaigns slower and more expensive.
